title: Herath's walnuts
hookLine: walnuts soaking in pots of water through Shiva's great night, then handed out to the neighbors
carry: Herath: Shiva's night ends in shared prasad
tomorrow: a king so good that the gods grew worried. who was he?
last: KHEER BHAWANI: THE MOTHER IS FED LIKE FAMILY.

cards: A kitchen in winter. On a clean cloth, a row of pots, filled to the brim with water, and in the water, walnuts, still in their shells. Someone has drawn on the pots and hung flowers around their necks.

The family will sit up with them tonight, singing, worshiping, keeping the lamp going. In a day or two, those walnuts will be soft from the water and on their way to every relative and neighbor on the list.
This is Herath, Shiva's great night, kept the Kashmiri way, and the last of the Kashmir days.

teach.b: You met Mahashivaratri in year one: the great night of Shiva, kept with fasting and worship and staying awake. Kashmiri Pandits keep it too, and they call it Herath.
In their tradition it's a night kept at home, around the family, more than at a temple.

The family sets out a pot and smaller vessels, filled with water and walnuts, and calls the arrangement the vatuk. It's worshiped as Shiva and the company around him. Families tell the meaning in different ways.
Some speak of Shiva's wedding to Parvati, with the pots as the wedding guests. Others speak of Bhairava, a fierce form of Shiva, appearing as light. Nobody has to settle it tonight.
When the worship is over, the soaked walnuts become prasad, and here's the teaching.

Prasad means grace: what was offered to God comes back blessed, and grace isn't meant to be kept on a shelf. It's handed on. So the walnuts go out: to grandparents, to cousins, to the family next door.
In the days after, people visit each other with greetings.

teach.h: THE NIGHT ENDS AT THE NEIGHBORS'
teach.b: The night that begins alone with God ends at other people's doors. It's the same reason a Hindu friend presses a sweet into your hand after a puja, and why it's polite to take it with your right hand and say thank you.
And that closes the week: from Pandharpur's spire to Kashmir's lake, its kings, a theater, a recognition, a spring, and last, a holy night with a kitchen at its center.

how: Kashmiri Pandit families keep Herath at home with an overnight worship of the vatuk, pots of water and walnuts honored as Shiva and his company, and afterward share the soaked walnuts with relatives and neighbors as prasad.

o: where walnuts are buried in the snow as a winter offering
where Shiva's night is kept only inside the great temples
where Herath is kept at home with pots of water and walnuts

games.q: Herath at home — tap the pairs.
p: Shiva's great night, the Kashmiri way

s: Herath is kept mostly at home, around the family's pots
the worship centers on the vatuk set out in the house.
every family tells the meaning of the pots the same way

the walnuts are kept by the family who worshiped

games.q: after a puja at a friend's house, her mom hands you a little box of prasad sweets. you don't love that sweet. what fits the teaching?
o: take it gladly and share what you can't eat: prasad is grace, passed on.
politely say no thanks; it's only food.
keep it unopened on a shelf so it stays holy.
games.why: prasad is what comes back from God, blessed. you receive it with thanks, and like Herath's walnuts, it's meant to travel.

practice: Let the room go quiet, the way a house goes quiet late on Herath. If you pray, say om namah shivaya slowly, out loud or under the breath, a few times. If you don't, sit with the quiet.
Then think of one person you'd hand a walnut to, and send them a short message tonight: a greeting, the way Kashmiri families visit after the night.

wordCard.voice: Kashmir. Today, Herath, Shiva's great night kept by Kashmiri Pandits, with pots of water and walnuts that become a gift for the neighbors. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a name of Shiva; some readers link the Kashmiri word Herath to Hara-ratri, 'Hara's night'.
